title: Portfolio and order pages slow, users logged out
summary: At 09:31 UTC a config reload on postgres-orders doubled work_mem (4 MB → 8 MB). Within ~40 minutes the database’s per‑query memory usage grew, exhausting connection slots and driving CPU to 100 %. The positions query used by portfolio-service slowed from ~20 ms to >1.8 s, causing massive cache‑misses, 2‑second SQL timeouts, and downstream 502/503 errors on /v1/portfolio. Connection‑slot exhaustion also produced FATAL errors. Some users were logged out because the edge‑gateway timed out while stalled on portfolio calls.

hypothesis.mechanism: Increasing work_mem doubles per‑query memory allocation. Concurrent portfolio-service queries (positions) now consume more RAM, hitting max_connections limit, causing connection‑slot FATAL errors and CPU saturation. Slow queries exceed the 2 s client timeout, leading to cache‑miss storms and downstream 502/503 errors.
predictions: Rolling back work_mem to 4 MB will immediately reduce active connections and CPU.
pg_stat_statements will show the positions query plan changing (e.g., hash aggregate spill) after the config change.

hypothesis.mechanism: A sudden surge of portfolio requests overwhelms the positions table, exhausting connections and CPU independent of any config change.
predictions: Request rate metrics for portfolio-service would show a sharp increase at ~10:13.
No config change would precede the metric inflection.

hypothesis.mechanism: Frequent checkpoints cause I/O contention, raising CPU and latency, leading to the observed symptoms.
predictions: Checkpoint frequency would increase sharply after 10:13.
I/O wait metrics would correlate with latency spikes.

hypothesis.mechanism: Auth-service failure forces logouts; portfolio slowness is a side‑effect of re‑auth traffic.
predictions: Auth-service logs would show errors or elevated latency at 10:13‑10:45.

facts.statement: Portfolio-service begins seeing massive cache‑misses for positions at 10:13:01 UTC (≈1,800/min) and falls back to postgres-orders.
Portfolio-service reports SQL timeout (2000 ms) on postgres-orders from 10:16:01 UTC onward (≈600 errors).
Postgres-orders logs show the positions query taking ~1.8 s from 10:14:01 UTC (≈1,260 occurrences).
Postgres-orders emits FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved… from 10:16:25 UTC (≈350 occurrences).
CPU utilisation on postgres-orders jumps from baseline 0.34 to ~1.0 (last minute 0.977).
Active connections rise from baseline ~73 to ~165 (last minute).
p99 query latency climbs from baseline ~18 ms to ~681 ms (last minute).
Config change on postgres-orders at 09:31:44 UTC raised work_mem from 4 MB to 8 MB (reload).
Orders-service shows a few slow SELECT on orders (~223 ms) between 09:51‑10:20 UTC – modest compared to positions query.

assumptions.statement: Raising work_mem from 4 MB to 8 MB increases per‑query memory consumption enough to exhaust max_connections slots and drive CPU higher.
assumptions.reason: Work_mem controls memory for sorts/hashes; larger value means each concurrent query uses more RAM, limiting concurrent connections and increasing CPU for memory management.

assumptions.statement: No external traffic surge occurred in the 10:00‑10:45 window that could independently explain the connection‑count jump.
assumptions.reason: No upstream service logs (portfolio, orders, edge‑gateway) show a request‑rate spike; the cache‑miss surge aligns with the config change.

assumptions.statement: The checkpoint‑frequency warning at 09:33 UTC is a pre‑existing condition, not the proximate cause of the 10:13‑10:45 collapse.
assumptions.reason: Checkpoint warning appears well before the sharp metric inflection and does not worsen after 10:13.

gaps.reason: Needed to confirm or rule out auth‑service failure as cause of logouts.

gaps.scope: postgres-orders pg_stat_statements / EXPLAIN ANALYZE for positions query
gaps.reason: To verify whether work_mem change altered the query plan (e.g., hash‑join spill).
To definitively rule out a traffic surge (H2).
To ensure no other config tweak contributed.

actions.description: Rollback work_mem on postgres-orders to 4 MB and reload.
actions.rationale: Config change is the strongest candidate; rollback is immediate and reversible.

actions.description: Temporarily increase max_connections (or superuser_reserved_connections) on postgres-orders.
actions.rationale: Alleviates ongoing connection‑slot FATAL errors while rollback propagates.

actions.description: Capture pg_stat_statements for the positions query before and after rollback; compare planner choices.
actions.rationale: Provides concrete proof that work_mem altered the execution plan.

actions.description: Add pre‑deploy guard: any work_mem (or similar memory‑affecting) change must pass a load‑test or canary on a read‑replica.
Review and size max_connections relative to peak connection count plus headroom for memory‑heavy queries.
actions.rationale: Ensures DB can absorb similar spikes without slot exhaustion.

actions.description: Enable alerting on postgres-orders/cpu_util > 0.85 AND active_connections > 1.5× baseline with a 2‑minute evaluation window.
actions.rationale: Gives earlier warning before user‑visible impact.

open_questions: Exact mechanism: does larger work_mem cause the planner to pick a hash‑aggregate that spills to temporary files, driving CPU, or does it simply increase per‑connection memory pressure leading to OOM‑style throttling?
Why is there a ~40‑minute latency between the config reload (09:31) and the first symptom (10:13)? Could be gradual connection‑pool growth as services re‑establish pools after the reload.

Root cause of user logouts: were they a direct result of gateway timeouts, or did the gateway drop sessions because it could not reach auth‑service while busy on portfolio calls? (Need auth‑service & edge‑gateway logs.)
Replica fail‑over feasibility: responder asked about failing over to the replica; replication lag stayed <1 s but we have not verified the replica carries the same work_mem setting.
